title: The man who fell to earth
blurb: Past Simple across a story told in sequence

SLIDES: Baumgartner’s journey started at 3.16 p.m., when the large balloon slowly lifted him up into space.
He slowly moved his seat forward out of his capsule.
He didn’t think about the beautiful view or breaking the speed record.
Then he jumped. But immediately something went wrong.
Baumgartner landed on his feet. He was so happy to be safe that he fell down on his knees.

Stage 3 · Grammar

Past Simple — the tense a story is told in

You know most of this already. The negative and the question are where it breaks.

Read these four sentences from today’s recording.
  • The balloon slowly lifted him up into space.
  • Then he jumped. Something went wrong.
  • He didn’t think about the view or the record.
  • Did he know he was in danger?
In the last two sentences, what happens to the main verb after didn’t and did?
The four forms
Verb typePositiveNegativeQuestion & short answer
Regular (+ -ed)He landed on his feet.He didn’t land in the sea.Did he land safely? — Yes, he did.
IrregularHe went up in a balloon.He didn’t go alone.Did he go alone? — No, he didn’t.
be — the exceptionThe balloon was enormous.It wasn’t small.Was it enormous? — Yes, it was.
With a question wordWhere did he land?  —  In the desert.   Why was he worried?  —  Because of the spin.
Relative clause recycledthe pilot who jumped · the balloon which lifted him · the desert where he landed
Spelling of -ed
  • + ed — land → landed, watch → watched
  • ends in -e, + d — dive → dived, move → moved
  • short verb, double the last letter — drop → dropped, stop → stopped
  • consonant + -y, y → i — carry → carried, try → tried
When you use it
  • a finished action at a finished time — He jumped at 5.37.
  • a sequence of events in a story — He opened the door, moved forwards and jumped.
  • a past state — The balloon was enormous.
  • Time words: yesterday · last week · in 2012 · two years ago · then · after that

The rule underneath: /ɪd/ only after -t or -d. Everywhere else it is /t/ or /d/, and it adds no extra syllable.

Past or present? Choose the form the time words need.
1He from the edge of space in 2012.

FORM. Regular verbs add -ed: land → landed, climb → climbed. Irregular verbs change and must be learned: go → went, fall → fell, take → took.

NEGATIVE AND QUESTION. Use didn’t + plain verb, did + person + plain verb. The past is already inside did, so the main verb loses it.

BE IS DIFFERENT. was / were need no did: He wasn’t ready. Were you there?

Not “He didn’t went”, not “Did he landed?”, not “I was go”.

Lesson 8 puts this tense against the Past Continuous.

FORM. Regular verbs add -ed — land → landed, climb → climbed, watch → watched. A verb that already ends in -e adds only -d (dive → dived), a short verb ending consonant–vowel–consonant doubles the last letter (drop → dropped), and a verb ending consonant + -y changes the y to i (carry → carried). Irregular verbs follow no rule at all; you learn them one by one: go → went, fall → fell, take → took, sit → sat, put → put.

MEANING AND USE. The Past Simple is for something finished, at a finished time. That time can be stated (in 2012, last week, two years ago, at 5.37) or simply understood from the story. It is the tense that carries a narrative forward: each verb is the next thing that happened. It also describes a past state — The balloon was enormous — where nothing is really “happening” at all.

WHEN NOT TO USE IT. If the time is not finished, or you do not say when, English often prefers a different tense. Compare He jumped in 2012 (finished, dated) with The record stands today (still true now). And do not use it for an action that was already in progress when something else happened — that is the Past Continuous, and it is Lesson 8.

NEGATIVE AND QUESTION. Both are built with did: He didn’t land in the sea · Did he land safely? The tense is carried by did, so the main verb goes back to its plain form. This is the single most common mistake at this level, and it is worth saying to yourself: one past form per sentence. Short answers repeat the helping verb and nothing else: Yes, he did. No, he didn’t.

BE IS THE EXCEPTION. was and were never take did. The negative is wasn’t / weren’t and the question simply swaps the order: He was ready → Was he ready?

THE SOUND OF -ED. One spelling, three sounds: watched /t/, climbed /d/, landed /ɪd/. Only -t and -d verbs take /ɪd/, and only those add a syllable. Nobody will misunderstand you if you get this wrong, but it is what makes a past-tense sentence sound English.

The four to watch: “He didn’t went” · “Did he landed?” · “I was go to school” · “Yes, he did jumped”.

Relative clauses from Unit 2 come back today — the pilot who jumped. And in Lesson 8 this tense meets the Past Continuous, which is what you use for the action that was already happening.

Full grammar reference — Past Simple

Form

Regularwork → worked · live → lived · stop → stopped · study → studied
Irregulargo → went · fall → fell · take → took · see → saw
NegativeI didn’t go · she didn’t see it
QuestionDid you go? · Where did she go?
Short answersYes, I did. / No, they didn’t.
beI / he was · you / we / they were · wasn’t, weren’t · Was he late?

Spelling and sound

-ed sounds three ways: worked /t/ · lived /d/ · wanted /ɪd/. Spelling: stop → stopped, study → studied, play → played.

When and why we use it

  • A finished action at a finished time: He jumped in 2012.
  • A sequence of events — this is the tense a story is told in.
  • Past states with was / were: The desert was completely still.
  • A repeated action in the past: I walked to school every day.

Signal words

yesterday · last week · in 2012 · two years ago · when I was ten · then, after that

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I didn’t went. → I didn’t go.Didn’t carries the past; the verb stays plain.
  • Did you saw it? → Did you see it?Same rule in questions.
  • He was go home. → He went home.No was with a past simple verb.
  • I have seen him yesterday. → I saw him yesterday.A finished time forces the Past Simple.

Don’t confuse it with

Past Simple names when. The Present Perfect does not — the full contrast comes in Lesson 17.

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

Two texts. The story from the ground, and what happened two years later.

Before you read: look at the picture and the title of Text A.

What do you think worried the ground team most? Choose one, then read and find out.

A prediction, not an answer.

Text A — The day I watched a man fall from the sky

I worked for the ground team at Roswell, New Mexico, on 14 October 2012. My job was small — I checked the radios — but I remember every minute.

We waited two weeks for the wind. On an earlier date in October the weather stopped us an hour before launch. Then, on the fourteenth, the desert was still.

At sunrise the balloon went up, enormous, with plastic thinner than a shopping bag. Inside the capsule sat Felix Baumgartner, the Austrian pilot who wanted to jump from the edge of space. The balloon lifted him for two and a half hours, up to almost 39 kilometres.

Then he opened the door and moved forwards onto the step. Nobody spoke. On my screen I saw the curve of the Earth behind him.

He jumped at 5.37 p.m.

For the first half-minute everything looked perfect. He fell towards the desert faster and faster and passed the speed of sound — the first person in history to do that outside an aircraft. Then he started to turn. He went round and round, and we could not stop him. The engineer next to me said nothing. I did not breathe.

Baumgartner pulled out of the spin himself: he pushed his arms backwards and dropped his head. Four minutes and nineteen seconds after he left the capsule, his parachute opened.

He landed on his feet in the desert, and then he fell onto his knees. The rescue team reached him in ninety seconds.

People always ask me the same question: did he know he was in danger? He knew. He climbed into that capsule anyway.

5 · Now read Text B.

Text B — Two years later, in the same desert

Two years after Baumgartner, a second man went up from the same corner of New Mexico — and almost nobody knew about it.

Alan Eustace was 57, an engineer, and a senior manager at Google. He paid for the project himself. He did not use a capsule at all. He simply hung underneath a helium balloon in a special suit, with a parachute on his back.

On 24 October 2014 the balloon lifted him for two and a half hours, up to 41,419 metres — about two and a half kilometres higher than Baumgartner. Then he cut himself loose. Ninety seconds later he passed the speed of sound. He opened his parachute at about 5,500 metres and landed in the desert fifteen minutes after he left the balloon.

Baumgartner’s team invited the world’s media. Eustace invited one journalist. His altitude record still stands today, and his suit is now in a museum in Washington.

Source note. Text A is written for this course: the events, dates and figures are from the public record of the Red Bull Stratos mission of 14 October 2012, and the narrator is invented to tell the story from the ground — no words are attributed to anyone who took part. Text B is an educational adaptation of reporting by the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale, the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum and NPR on the StratEx jump of 24 October 2014.

Tell it in order

A short true story from your own life, told step by step.

Useful language

First…  Then…  After that…  A few minutes later…  In the end…

These five words hold a story together. Use at least three of them.
